analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to buy FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada, with safety and licensing rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2004 with eight Republican cosponsors and never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal drug law so Americans could legally import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada for personal use — up to a 90-day supply, carried on their person, with a valid prescription. After one year, licensed pharmacies, Internet pharmacies, and wholesalers could also import Canadian drugs for dispensing in the U.S., with labeling, tracking, and anti-counterfeiting requirements. It also creates a licensing system for Internet pharmacies and lets regulators block or detain shipments that appear unsafe. Canada caps what its government pays for drugs, so the same FDA-approved medicine often costs far less there than in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs — especially seniors and people without insurance coverage — would gain a legal way to buy the same FDA-approved medicines at Canadian prices. Internet and storefront pharmacies would gain a new, legal importation business line.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals could import up to a 90-day supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada for personal use, carried on their person, with a valid prescription [S2][S3].

One year after enactment, licensed pharmacies, Internet pharmacies, and wholesalers could import Canadian drugs for dispensing in the United States, opening a commercial channel for lower-cost medicines [S2][S3].
The Secretary of Health and Human Services could designate additional European Union countries as sources after three years, expanding the supply of lower-priced drugs [S2][S3].

The bill pairs importation with safety tools: FDA detention of risky shipments, suspension of importers that violate the rules, Internet pharmacy licensing, and anti-counterfeiting provisions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose revenue from the price gap between U.S. and Canadian prices. Payment card networks and online advertising providers would bear the cost of building systems to block transactions and ads tied to unlicensed Internet pharmacies, and could face liability if they fail. The FDA and taxpayers would bear the cost of inspecting shipments and enforcing the new licensing and registration system, funded partly by user fees on importers and a $5,000 initial Internet pharmacy licensing fee.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and card networks

drawbacks.text: The importation right excludes biologic and biotechnology drugs, refrigerated drugs, and other categories, so many newer and more expensive medicines could not be imported at all [S3].
Personal importation is limited to a 90-day supply carried on the person, so patients could not simply have larger orders shipped from Canada under this provision [S2][S3].

The bill imposes liability on advertising providers and payment systems for transactions tied to unlicensed pharmacies, a compliance burden those industries would pass on in cost and friction [S2][S3].

Enforcement is expensive: the bill creates registration, record-keeping, advance-notice, and port-inspection regimes, and gives the Secretary power to suspend imports entirely if a safety pattern emerges — meaning the price savings depend on regulators building a system that can distinguish safe shipments from counterfeits [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients paying U.S. prices, the potential savings are real: the same FDA-approved pills are routinely cheaper in Canada because of Canadian price controls. The bill tries to capture those savings while building guardrails against counterfeit or unsafe drugs, and it reasonably excludes the hardest-to-verify categories like biologics. The honest cost is that the safety apparatus — fees, inspections, and liability rules — adds expense and complexity, and the narrow personal-importation rules limit how much a typical patient could actually save. It was a cautious version of importation, not a wide-open one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 2, 2004, read twice, and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Senator Judd Gregg, a Republican from New Hampshire, introduced the Safe IMPORT Act on June 2, 2004 [S1][S2].
Eight Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill died there when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers came out ahead: the bill that would have opened a legal channel for cheaper Canadian medicines never advanced, leaving the U.S.-only pricing structure untouched. American consumers — particularly seniors and the uninsured — lost the chance the bill offered.

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire and sponsor of S. 2493
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 2, 2004, authorizing personal and commercial importation of FDA-approved drugs from Canada

for.name: 8 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors of S. 2493 (including Sens. Smith, Collins, Coleman, Sessions, Lott, and Enzi)

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed drug importation legislation and campaigned on safety and counterfeit-drug risks during the period when Congress considered importation bills

sides.party_line_note: All eight cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill would let pharmacies and individuals import the same FDA-approved drugs at Canadian government-negotiated prices, eroding the higher U.S. prices manufacturers charge. The bill's death preserved that price gap.

industries.industry: Internet and retail pharmacies and drug wholesalers
industries.note: Licensed pharmacies, Internet pharmacies, and wholesalers would gain a new legal importation business, though they would pay registration and user fees and a $5,000 initial Internet pharmacy license and follow labeling and record-keeping rules.

industries.industry: Credit card networks and payment processors
industries.note: They would be required to build systems that identify and block payments to unlicensed Internet pharmacies and would face enforcement exposure if they fail, though the bill shields them from liability when they block transactions in good faith.

Providers would become liable for accepting ads from unlicensed Internet pharmacies or ads claiming prescription drugs are available without a prescription, and could be ordered to disable violating websites.
